entry.title: A battle-tested SRE’/Devops Engineers guide to our robot-assisted future
entry.summary: In the old days, this meant stumbling to your laptop, squinting at logs that might as well be hieroglyphics, and playing a delightful game of “Was it certificate expiry? It’s always certificate expiry. Wait, maybe it’s the load? Or did Jerry push something to prod again?” But here’s the plot twist that would make George R. Martin jealous: My AI-powered monitoring system had already identified the root cause, suggested a fix, and was politely asking if I wanted it to automatically rollback the problematic deployment. I felt like Neo seeing the Matrix code for the first time, except instead of green cascading numbers, it was beautifully formatted incident reports. Welcome to 2025, where artificial intelligence isn’t just writing poetry and generating questionable content—it’s keeping your infrastructure running while you sleep. And honestly? I’m only slightly concerned about our future robot overlords. At least they’ll have excellent observability. This isn’t another breathless “AI will save/destroy us all” hot take. This is a field report from the trenches, where AI has quietly become the most valuable team member who never complains about being on-call and actually reads the documentation.

entry.title: When nobody should have invested
entry.summary:
I examined 6 startups whose members deceived their investors in some way. The 6 startups were: Theranos, WeWork, Nikola Motors, builder.ai, FTX, Frank. The primary goal of the investigation was to determine what the early signs and common features are that would indicate that the startup is fraudulent. I found 3 such signs. One telltale sign is that a startup's early marketing mix is disproportionately heavy on PR. The founders of such startups are going from studio to studio and conference to conference. And here, alongside our main question, arises why journalists believe them. Another telltale sign is that the startup does not appear to pose a threat to the established companies in its market. For example, Uber poses a major threat to traditional taxi services, while WeWork itself did not pose a threat to office publishing companies.
And the third is that they have connections to famous people and it's even possible that they have insiders at big companies that are looking to them to be investors. The second half of the claim is just a hunch for now, I can't prove it. There are 3 main reasons why investors don't notice when a startup founder cheats. Reasons that are known in psychology. So I don't blame them. The vast majority of people would do the same as investors. I will write about these three reasons in my next post.
